Opening poll

Which task would you hand over?

Then discuss

What would the robot need to prove before you trusted it?

Missed dirt is inconvenient; unsafe driving or a surgical error can cause serious harm. Convenience matters. So do the consequences of a mistake. We revisit your choice on the last slide.
AI × Robotics · Week 10A02 / 40

Interactive: One click per raised hand; right-click undoes. Ask two students with different choices to explain.

Give students one minute to choose, then ask two students with different choices to explain. Encourage concrete criteria: missed dirt is inconvenient, while unsafe driving or a surgical error can cause serious harm. Revisit these choices on the final slide. There is no single correct ranking because people have different needs and circumstances.

Products, services, and clinical systems

The scope of everyday robotics

Where we meet a robotExamples in this survey
At homeVacuum-mops, mowers, pool cleaners, cooking devices
Through a serviceRobotaxis and sidewalk delivery
In a clinicRobotic guidance for dental implant surgery
In early developmentHumanoid housekeepers and stair-climbing vacuums

A robot may be useful without looking human.

AI × Robotics · Week 10A03 / 40

The word consumer describes who benefits, not necessarily who owns the hardware. A household may buy a vacuum, summon a robotaxi, and receive treatment from a clinician who operates a robotic system. Avoid comparing those business models as if they were all store-bought appliances. This scope intentionally extends beyond traditional consumer electronics.

Sense, plan, act, check

The robot’s repeating loop

01 · Sense

Cameras and other sensors estimate what is nearby.

02 · Plan

Software chooses a route or a useful next action.

03 · Act

Motors move wheels, brushes, hands, or instruments.

04 · Check

New sensor readings reveal whether the action worked.

AI × Robotics · Week 10A04 / 40

Interactive: Press “One phase” four times to walk one loop: sense the neighbours, plan a path to the nearest dirty square, move, mark it clean. Then Run.

Use a vacuum approaching a chair leg: it observes an obstacle, chooses a path, moves, and checks again. This loop connects to the course’s agentic workflow discussion. Physical actions introduce friction, delays, collisions, and wear. A spoken plan alone cannot guarantee that a motor will perform the intended movement. Exact sensor and control designs differ across products.

Floor care

Vacuuming and mopping in one trip

The everyday job

A mobile cleaner maps rooms, collects debris, and wipes hard floors using a wet cleaning system.

The remaining work

People still prepare the space, deal with unusual messes, and maintain the robot and its dock.

Photo: Spider’s Web

AI × Robotics · Week 10A07 / 40

Use the photograph of a Saros 20 crossing a threshold to ask what can interrupt a routine cleaning job. Mixed flooring, cables, loose fabric, and clutter change the task. Vacuuming removes dry debris, while mopping uses contact and moisture. Neither function guarantees hygienic disinfection or removal of every stain. Floor and cleaning-solution compatibility follow the product instructions.

Dust

Ask students to estimate the work saved across a month rather than during a single cleaning run. Some docks require manual tank refills, while particular installations or models support plumbing. Pair discussion · 2 minutes

The apartment obstacle test

A vacuum-mop sees four things. Which should it clean, avoid, or ask about? What could go wrong if it guesses?

A charging cableStop before pulling or tangling it. Recognizing the cable is not enough — the robot needs a safe action.
A dark rugDepends on the household’s settings and floor compatibility — mopping a rug may be wrong.
A spilled drinkAn unknown liquid could damage the robot or spread the mess. Ask a person.
A pet’s toyDriving into it could push or swallow it. The same object can matter differently in different homes.
A useful robot needs a sensible response to uncertainty.
AI × Robotics · Week 10A12 / 40

Give pairs two minutes. The exercise is conceptual, not product operating advice. A good answer may be to avoid unknown liquids, respect floor compatibility, and stop before pulling a cable. The point is that object recognition alone is insufficient: the robot also needs an appropriate action. The same visible object can have different significance in different households.

Outdoor robotics

Lawn mowing within a boundary

The robot needs to know where mowing is allowed.

Older designs

A buried perimeter wire marks the edge.

Newer designs

Satellite positioning with corrections, cameras, lidar, or combinations follow a virtual boundary.

The owner’s map

Work areas and exclusion zones are drawn in an app — but must match the real yard.

A digital boundary still depends on a real yard.

AI × Robotics · Week 10A13 / 40

Some mowers use a perimeter wire. Newer wire-free designs can use satellite positioning with corrections, cameras, lidar, or combinations. A map lets an owner specify work areas and exclusion zones. Real edges, roads, water, slopes, and obstructions still require careful setup. Satellite reception and local perception are complementary rather than interchangeable.

Mower reality check

A lawn is more than open grass

Yard conditionWhy it matters
Trees and buildingsThey can obstruct satellite signals or views.
Slopes and wet groundTraction and stopping distance change.
Children, pets, wildlifeDetection must lead to safe stopping or avoidance.
Edges and narrow passagesThe route needs enough clearance and a safe boundary.
Your yard

Picture a yard you know. Which feature would be hardest for a robot mower?

Useful automation begins with a suitable operating area. An obstacle-recognition claim never justifies letting children or animals near operating blades.

Weather meets robotics

Snow changes the problem

Material

Light powder, wet snow, and ice behave differently.

Visibility

Falling snow and buildup can affect sensors.

Movement

Traction, slopes, and buried obstacles change the route.

Discharge

Thrown snow must stay clear of people and property.

Connect to Week 7

How could a weather forecast help schedule a snow robot’s work?

Clearing fresh snowfall often is easier than attacking a compacted pile left by a road plow — a forecast lets the robot work before the problem gets harder.
AI × Robotics · Week 10A18 / 40

A snow robot works on changing material rather than a stable floor. These are general engineering considerations, not a measured failure rate for Yarbo. Compare removing fresh snowfall frequently with confronting a compacted pile from a road plow. For operation, the product manual governs suitable snow conditions, safety distances, cleaning, and intervention. Ask how a weather forecast could help schedule work.

Group scenario · 4 minutes

An Albany winter morning

Click each area: Work → Exclude → Ask first

Where could a robot work? Where should it stop or request help? What would a person check first?

Work: the flat driveway, cleared often while snow is fresh.
Exclude: around the parked car, and never throw snow toward the sidewalk.
Ask first: the steep, possibly icy section.
Stop condition: a person — especially a child — enters the work zone. Check first: buried objects.

The environment helps define the robot’s job.

AI × Robotics · Week 10A19 / 40

Interactive: Groups label each zone, then compare with the suggested plan. Hypothetical planning only — not operating advice.

This is a hypothetical planning activity, not an instruction to operate equipment. Have groups identify a work zone, an exclusion zone, and one stop condition. Good answers consider buried objects, snow discharge, sidewalk access, icy surfaces, and people arriving unexpectedly. Ask what information a robot needs before starting and how it should respond when those conditions change.

Who is responsible for the driving?

Driver assistance and driverless service

Who watches the road?
The human driver, continuously.
Who handles problems?
The driver takes over at any moment.
Where does it work?
Wherever the driver chooses to use it — the driver stays responsible.
Who watches the road?
The system, within its defined conditions.
Who handles problems?
The system handles driving and fallback within its domain.
Where does it work?
Only inside its operational design domain: limited geography, roads, speeds, or weather.

Automation level describes responsibility and operating limits. A product called “self-driving” does not establish its level.

AI × Robotics · Week 10A24 / 40

Interactive: Toggle the two levels and read the three answers. Conceptual comparison, not legal advice.

NHTSA distinguishes partial automation from high automation. At Level 2, a driver monitors the environment and remains responsible. A Level 4 system handles driving and fallback within its operational design domain. That domain can limit geography, road types, speeds, or weather. A product name containing self-driving does not establish a level of autonomy. This slide is a conceptual comparison, not legal advice.

NHTSA, Automated Vehicle Safety and levels of automation. https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/automated-vehicle-safety

Accessed October 11, 2026.

Robotaxi discussion

What would count as safety evidence?

Exposure

How many miles, on which roads, in what conditions?

Outcomes

Injuries and serious incidents matter more than a demo.

Comparison

Human and automated driving need comparable conditions.

Support

Stopping, remote assistance, and emergency response matter.

Raw counts are not risk. What denominator do you need? Hypothetical numbers.

AI × Robotics · Week 10A25 / 40

Waymo publishes safety research and exposure data. NHTSA collects certain crash reports, but raw counts alone do not provide a fair risk comparison because exposure, reporting rules, and operating conditions differ. Ask students what denominator they would need. Remote assistance also requires precise language: help interpreting a situation differs from a human continuously steering a vehicle.

Research / prototype

Perceptive explores robotic restorative care

Imaging, planning, and action

The company combines optical imaging with AI and a robotic system aimed at restorative dental procedures.

Development status

Its website describes a system under development. Speed targets and demonstrations do not establish routine clinical availability.

Photo: Perceptive

AI × Robotics · Week 10A27 / 40

Perceptive describes optical coherence tomography for three-dimensional imaging and a robotics program focused on restorative procedures. The site explicitly labels prototype imagery and states that the system is being developed. Do not repeat its targeted procedure time as a proven clinical outcome. Distinguish an engineering demonstration, clinical evidence, regulatory authorization, and deployment in ordinary practice.

Clinical responsibility

The dental team remains central

Part of careWhy human expertise remains essential
Diagnosis and consentThe clinician explains options and determines suitability.
PlanningThe team evaluates anatomy and the treatment plan.
ProcedureThe clinician monitors the patient and can intervene.
Follow-upHealing and outcomes require continuing care.

Precision in one movement is only one part of good care.

AI × Robotics · Week 10A28 / 40

Use the table to separate a robot’s technical contribution from the wider clinical process. Robotic guidance can constrain movement, while diagnosis, consent, management of complications, and follow-up remain clinical responsibilities. The FDA’s intended-use description supports assistance rather than autonomous practice. Avoid claiming that all patients benefit equally or that a regulatory clearance proves superiority over every alternative.

The challenge of generality

Why housekeeping is so difficult

“Tidy the room” hides many different tasks.

A robot must decide what belongs where, handle unfamiliar objects, and move safely around people.

A towel changes shape. A glass can break. A person can move.

Making a bed: the hidden decisions

  1. Infer the goal: what does “made” mean in this home?
  2. Recognize the sheet, blanket, and pillows
  3. Choose a grasp on soft, shape-changing fabric
  4. Coordinate both arms and the body
  5. Recover when the sheet slips
  6. Move safely if someone walks in
AI × Robotics · Week 10A29 / 40

Interactive: Ask the class to list hidden decisions first, then reveal.

Contrast floor coverage with an open-ended housekeeping request. The robot must infer a goal, recognize objects, choose grasps, coordinate its body, and recover when something slips. Homes differ in layout and social rules. A foundation model may improve transfer, but task completion still depends on sensors, mechanics, training, and safe control. Students can list hidden decisions in making a bed.

Figure’s September 17, 2026 report compares a pretrained model with a model trained from scratch on the same task data. The company reports 56% versus 9% success across its evaluation. Different paths to useful work

Specialized appliances and home humanoids

Specialized robot

One job

A limited task in a prepared environment.

General home robot

Many jobs

Many tasks in changing, shared spaces.

Breadth of ambition increases the burden of testing.

Vote · what would your household prefer?

What evidence would change your vote?
AI × Robotics · Week 10A32 / 40

This is a synthesis of the examples rather than a scorecard. A constrained task can still be technically challenging, and specialized products can fail. Generality adds variation in objects, goals, people, and recovery. Ask whether a household would prefer several affordable specialist machines or one flexible helper, and what evidence would change that preference.

Comparison across applications

The work robots leave for people

ApplicationHuman work around the robot
Floor and yard careSet boundaries, prepare the area, maintain equipment
Robotaxi and deliveryOperate the service, support exceptions, manage access
Dental proceduresMake clinical decisions and monitor patient care
Kitchen and housekeepingPrepare inputs, specify goals, handle uncertain cases

The surrounding workflow determines how much help a robot provides.

AI × Robotics · Week 10A37 / 40

This table is a synthesis rather than a benchmark ranking. Ask students to evaluate the full workflow: setup, routine use, exceptions, maintenance, and eventual repair. A robot can reduce physical strain or create access even when it does not eliminate all labor. The best measure of usefulness depends on the user’s needs and the cost of mistakes.

Questions for any connected robot

Privacy and safety follow the robot home

Data

What do cameras, microphones, and maps capture?

Access

Who can view data or remotely control the device?

Failure

What happens during a jam, outage, or lost connection?

Lifetime

Can the owner repair it and keep receiving support?

Before you buy, can you answer…

These are questions, not allegations about any company.

AI × Robotics · Week 10A38 / 40

A robot may record sensitive details about rooms, routines, or people nearby. The exact data path varies by product, so read the product policy rather than assuming all processing is local or cloud based. Remote access should be visible and governed by consent. Physical stop mechanisms, safe behavior when disconnected, software support, and repairability are all part of evaluating a product. These are questions, not allegations about any company.

Small-group design challenge · 5 minutes

A robot for one useful task

Your one-minute pitch card

A convincing proposal includes the difficult cases.

AI × Robotics · Week 10A39 / 40

Interactive: Groups fill the eight fields; project the pitch card for one-minute pitches. A modest, testable job beats a robot that promises everything.

Allow five minutes, then invite one-minute pitches. Encourage accessible use cases such as reaching a difficult cleaning area or reducing repetitive lifting. Assess the clarity of the user need, the operating boundary, the failure response, and the proposed evidence. A modest system with a testable job can make a stronger proposal than a robot that promises to do everything.

Takeaways and exit question

What should we expect from everyday robots?

Capability
AI helps robots perceive and adapt to physical situations.
Boundaries
Useful autonomy always has conditions and limits.
Workflow
Human setup, maintenance, and support still matter.
Your choice
Which opening task would you delegate now, and why? Cite one product and one limitation.
AI × Robotics · Week 10A40 / 40

Return to the opening poll. Ask students to cite one specific product example and one limitation in their answer. They should distinguish a commercial product, a local service, a preorder, and a research result. Further reading: current manufacturer pages linked throughout the notes, the FDA Yomi S record, NHTSA’s automation-level overview, and Figure’s evaluation report. Recheck commercial availability and deployment areas before reuse.
